## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (“The Fruits of the Ascetic Life”, DN 2) is the second discourse of the *Dīgha Nikāya*, preserved in the *Sīlakkhandhavagga* [MacQueen 1988; Chen 2015]. The narrative is set on a moonlit night in Rājagaha, where King Ajātasattu of Magadha, troubled after acquiring the crown through patricide, visits the Buddha to inquire into the tangible, visible benefits of ascetic life (*sāmaññaphala*) [Allon, Senior Manuscripts; Wu 2012; Chen 2015]. Ajātasattu explains that he previously posed this inquiry to six rival non-Buddhist teachers (including Makkhali Gosāla and his doctrine of non-causality), but received no satisfactory reply [Allon, Senior Manuscripts; Law 1931; Wu 2012; Chen 2015; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. In response, the Buddha expounds the gradual path of monastic training—progressing from ethical discipline (*sīla*) and sense restraint, through the abandonment of the five hindrances (illustrated with five similes), to the four *jhāna*s, higher knowledges, and final liberation [Anālayo 2014; Shulman 2014]. Converted, the king confesses his crime; Buddhaghosa’s commentary notes that hearing this sermon mitigates Ajātasattu's karmic retribution in hell and ensures his future liberation as a *paccekabuddha* [Wu 2012; Chen 2015].
